rapidFireQAs.a: Benign; can be unilateral or bilateral; classic textbook description is “bilateral breast pain/tenderness that waxes/wanes with menstrual cycle,” but Obgyn forms can have it presenting as unilateral pain, or as a unilateral painless cyst that drains dark fluid; no treatment is necessary most of the time; if patient has a singularly enlarged cyst that appears after starting hormone-replacement therapy, FNA is the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about menstrual cycle / pregnancy hormones?
rapidFireQAs.a: First half of menstrual cycle = proliferative/follicular phase; second half = luteal/secretory phase. The luteal phase is always 14 days; if menstrual cycle changes length, it’s because of variation in the follicular phase. Estrogen gradually increases throughout the follicular phase and is highest just prior to ovulation, then it declines after. The high estrogen causes an LH spike that triggers ovulation. The corpus luteum is the follicular remnant and produces progesterone that maintains the endometrial lining during the luteal phase. If pregnancy occurs, b-hCG will maintain the corpus luteum, which will enable continued progesterone production so the pregnancy can be maintained. If pregnancy does not occur and b-hCG is not present, the corpus luteum degrades, progesterone production ceases, and sloughing of the endometrium occurs (menstruation). As discussed earlier, b-hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks of pregnancy. After this point, the placenta takes over production of progesterone, so we no longer need hCG to maintain the corpus luteum. Human placental lactogen (hPL) is a hormone that increases during third trimester of pregnancy and causes insulin resistance in the mother. This ensures that glucose levels are high enough so that brain development in the fetus occurs properly. The tradeoff is that this is the hormone that increases risk of gestational diabetes. Prolactin produced by the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. Oxytocin produced by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus (and stored in the posterior pituitary) causes milk letdown (release). It also stimulates uterine contractions.

rapidFireQAs.q: Do I need to know anything about Tanner stages?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tanner stages 1-5 are a system for genital/breast development. You don’t need to know the strict Tanner stages, just a few key factoids. For whatever reason, it’s exceedingly HY on 2CK Obgyn forms that you know once a female hits Tanner stage 3, menarche is imminent (meaning, will occur very soon); they ask this directly in one Q; they also incorporate it into other Qs. For instance, they’ll say a 14-year-old girl who’s never had a menstrual period is brought in by her mom + she is Tanner stage 3 + they ask for next step in management → answer = follow-up in 6 months (since she’s Tanner stage 3, we know menarche is imminent, so we’ll just wait it out). Low Tanner stage (i.e., 1 or 2) can be the USMLE’s way of telling you a boy or girl has constitutional short stature (i.e., will achieve normal height, but has growth curve that is delayed / shifted to the right). For instance, they can say a boy is shortest in his class freshman year of high school + is Tanner stage 1 → answer = constitutional short stature. This diagnosis is also made where bone age is less than chronologic age. If bone age = chronologic age, then the short stature is genuine. Turner syndrome classically has Tanner stage 1-2 breasts (i.e., “shield chest”), but it is not mandatory the Tanner stage is low on Obgyn material.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about precocious puberty?
rapidFireQAs.a: Emergence of secondary sex characteristics in females age 8 or younger, or males 9 or younger. Childhood height will be increased; adult height will be decreased. Question might ask how we know if the cause of the precocious puberty is due to the hypothalamus/pituitary axis or not → answer = if LH is high (if LH low, we know cause is primary testicular production of testosterone). If DHEA-S is abnormally high, we know the adrenal gland is the cause (the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex secretes DHEA-S and androstenedione).

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about imperforate hymen?
rapidFireQAs.a: Will present as bluish bulge behind hymen in female who’s never had a menstrual period; they can describe Hx of cyclical pain (due to menses with blood backup behind the hymen). Hematocolpos = blood backed up in the vaginal canal behind the hymen. Hematometra = blood backed up all the way to the uterine cavity, precipitating and vagal response and low blood pressure.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is placenta previa?
rapidFireQAs.a: Placental implantation site over the internal cervical os. Causes third-trimester painless bleeding. Can spontaneously move off the os prior the 36 weeks’ gestation; after this point, C-section must be done, otherwise patient may experience hemorrhagic shock during parturition. USMLE wants you to know that prior C-section is a risk factor for placenta previa (i.e., if the endometrial lining has been disturbed in the past in any way, then that simply increases the risk of an abnormal implantation).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is abruptio placentae?
rapidFireQAs.a: Abruption (separation) of the placenta in utero. Causes third-trimester painful bleeding, or painful cramping. Deceleration injury (i.e., car accident, fall) and cocaine use are known risk factors.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is placenta accrete/increta/percreta?
rapidFireQAs.a: Presents as postpartum bleeding/hemorrhage. Accreta = placenta attaches to surface of myometrium. A = attaches. Increta = placenta inserts into/inside myometrium. I = inserts inside. Percreta = placenta perforates through myometrium and attaches onto external structures, such as the bladder. P = perforates.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is most common cause of postpartum bleeding?
rapidFireQAs.a: Uterine atony → presents as boggy uterus postpartum; Tx with uterine massage, followed by intra-myometrial oxytocin injection, followed by ergotamine injection (avoid the latter if HTN or migraine Hx). Less common causes are retained placental parts (if they tell you all lobes of placenta are not present), vaginal lacerations (e.g., from macrosomia in maternal diabetes, where the fetus experienced shoulder dystocia), or thrombotic disorders (e.g., von Willebrand).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is vasa previa?
rapidFireQAs.a: When the fetal vessels overly the internal cervical os. Normally, the vessels are protected by Wharton jelly within the umbilical cord, but sometimes the vessels can be abnormally exposed in the setting of velamentous cord insertion, or if there is the presence of a succenturiate lobe of the placenta. Presents as triad of 1) rupture of membranes; 2) vaginal bleeding; 3) fetal bradycardia.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about ectopic pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: Can present as LLQ or LRQ pain in female who has a missed menstrual period. b-hCG will be positive, but the numerical value will be described as a lot lower than expected. This is in contrast to hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma, where the b-hCG is much higher than expected. Methotrexate can be given for small, stable ectopics. Otherwise, laparoscopic salpingostomy is performed. If the patient is unstable (i.e., low BP in ruptured ectopic), laparotomy is the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is preclampsia, eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: Preeclampsia = HTN and proteinuria after 20 weeks’ gestation. That is the most simplified definition and sufficient for USMLE. Eclampsia = preeclampsia + seizure. Tx = magnesium as Tx (and prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia). HELLP syndrome = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count. Severe manifestation of preeclampsia. Schistocytes are seen on a blood smear.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is supine hypotensive syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: Low blood pressure in woman >20 weeks’ gestation due to compression of IVC.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about endometriosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Endometrial tissue growing outside the uterus, usually on the ovary; can cause severely painful periods; descriptors such as pain with defecation or dyspareunia are often too buzzy and omitted from questions. Physical examination will be abnormal (e.g., nodularity of uterosacral ligaments); patient can get hemorrhagic (“chocolate”) cysts; diagnosis is done via exploratory laparoscopy. Treatment is with OCPs +/- NSAIDs. Definitive is laparoscopic removal of lesions.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about primary dysmenorrhea?
rapidFireQAs.a: This is “normal period pain” due to prostaglandin secretion; physical examination is normal, in contrast to endometriosis. Treatment is with NSAIDs. Don’t confuse with mittelschmerz, which is ovulatory pain mid-cycle.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is adenomyosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Diffusely enlarged uterus in woman generally 30s-40s, often with vaginal bleeding. They can say a woman had a tubule ligation 2 years ago, but now has vaginal bleeding with a uterus that is 8 weeks’ gestation in size. Treatment is with OCPs + NSAIDs.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about BPH?
rapidFireQAs.a: Prostatic enlargement occurs as a result of DHT stimulation. USMLE loves post-renal obstruction due to BPH causing “increased tubular hydrostatic pressure,” or “increased Bowman capsule hydrostatic pressure” in the setting of high creatinine.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about HY Repro pharm?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tamoxifen + raloxifene are selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs). They can be used in ER(+) breast cancer. They are antagonists at breast + agonists at bone. Highest yield point is that tamoxifen is partial agonist at endometrium → increased risk of endometrial cancer. Never give tamoxifen to woman who has a uterus. Give raloxifene instead. Anastrozole + exemestane are aromatase inhibitors. These can be used in breast cancer. Trastuzumab (Herceptin) targets HER2/neu(+) breast cancer. It is cardiotoxic. Clomiphene is partial agonist at the hypothalamus (the effect is as though it’s an antagonist). This stimulates GnRH secretion → promotes ovulation. It is used in women who have abnormal periods, where ovulation is difficult to predict. Or it can be used in IVF. Mifepristone is a progesterone receptor antagonist used as an abortifacient. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue used with mifepristone as an abortifacient. Ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator used as emergency contraception. Dinoprostone is a prostaglandin E2 analogue used to soften the cervix. Ritodrine is a beta-2 agonist used as a tocolytic. Danazol is an androgen receptor partial agonist used as a tertiary agent in endometriosis. However it is one of the first-line agents for hereditary angioedema (causes liver to produce more C1 esterase inhibitor). Combined estrogen oral contraceptive pills → contraindicated in women who are smokers over 35, have migraine with aura, active breast cancer, or Hx of thrombotic disorders / DVT. Finasteride is a 5a-reductase inhibitor that prevents the conversion of testosterone to DHT in the treatment of BPH. Tamsulosin and terasozin are a1-antagonists used in the treatment of BPH. They relieve constriction of the internal urethral sphincter. Leuprolide is a GnRH receptor agonist that, when given continuously, causes desensitization of the GnRH receptor, thereby effectively acting as an antagonist. This causes a reduction in LH and FSH. It is used for prostate cancer. It can also be used for adenomyosis and fibroids, albeit not first line. Flutamide is an androgen receptor antagonist used in the treatment of prostate cancer. This is given prior to leuprolide, since the latter will cause a transient increase in LH and FSH prior to desensitization of the GnRH receptor. The transient increase in LH can theoretically cause a transient increase in testosterone, so flutamide must be given first to block receptors. Oxybutynin is a muscarinic receptor antagonist used in the treatment of urge incontinence. Bethanechol is a muscarinic receptor agonist used in the treatment of overflow incontinence due to diabetes (neurogenic / hypotonic bladder). If the cause of the overflow incontinence is BPH, however, the BPH itself must be treated first as per above.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + not breastfeeding + upper-outer quadrant warm, tender, red non-fluctuant mass +/- fever; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = mastitis, not breast abscess; the key here is non-fluctuant mass; abscess is identical presentation but fluctuant. For mastitis, the easier, Step 1 presentation is the standard red, cracked, fissured nipple in a breastfeeding woman → S. aureus → Tx = continue breastfeeding through the affected breast; can give oral dicloxacillin (answer on newer Obgyn form) or cephalexin for mastitis; for abscess, answer = always drain before Abx.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + recently stopped breastfeeding + temp 99.5F + tender, fluctuant mass in lateral breast + not warm + not erythematous; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = galactocele (milk retention cyst); classically subareolar or in lateral breast; Tx on Obgyn NBME is warm compresses (“application of heat to the area”).

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + gave birth two days ago + exclusively bottle-feeding neonate + breasts are engorged and tender + fever of 101F + Sx of dysuria + suprapubic tenderness + urinalysis normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = breast engorgement → every student gets this wrong because it sounds like obvious infection; learning point is: can present with fever; occasional Sx of dysuria + normal U/A are not atypical in women.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + amenorrhea since D&C 13 months ago for postpartum hemorrhage + progestin withdrawal test shows no withdrawal bleeding; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Asherman syndrome or “uterine synechiae” on Obgyn shelf.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + spontaneous abortion at 10 weeks’ gestation complicated by postpartum endometritis + sharp D/C to remove infected material; patient is subsequently at increased risk for what?
rapidFireQAs.a: amenorrhea (Asherman syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does progestin withdrawal test mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: if progestin is given then withdrawn, bleeding should occur (hormonal stabilization of lining followed by allowing it to slough, akin to forcing a menstruation); if bleeding occurs, estrogen is not deficient and the Dx is anovulation (PCOS is just anovulation leading to 11+ cysts bilaterally + hirsutism; anovulation as independent term is same mechanism as full-blown PCOS) → if anovulation occurs, there’s no corpus luteum and therefore no progesterone released → cannot establish endogenous rise + fall of progestin, therefore no sloughing/menstruation; in contrast, if bleeding does not occur with progestin withdrawal test, either estrogen is deficient (primary ovarian failure or hypogonadotropic disorder) or the uterus is scarred (Asherman).

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + no bleeding after progestin withdrawal test; Q asks, if not Tx over ten years, what is patient at risk for?
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoporosis (progestin withdrawal result means low estrogen).

rapidFireQAs.q: Question shows you a graph where basal body temperature increases ~0.5F mid-cycle and stays at this higher temp; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: progesterone (ovulation).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + she asks about best way to decrease risk of osteoporosis
rapidFireQAs.a: weight-bearing exercise, not calcium + vitamin D.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72F + already has osteoporosis + Q asks best way to most greatly decrease fracture risk
rapidFireQAs.a: going on long walks; wrong answer is swimming / pool exercises (weight-bearing component makes sense, but actually tricky considering elderly have high falls risk).

rapidFireQAs.q: 69F + Caucasian + nulliparous + on beta-blocker + drinks daily + compression fracture of vertebra; what is strongest predisposing risk factor (family Hx not discussed or listed)?
rapidFireQAs.a: race; white race confers higher risk of osteoporosis; wrong answers are alcohol use, beta-blocker, nulliparity, HTN.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + 8-month Hx of severe pelvic pain and heavy bleeding during menses + regular periods + two kids + does not want more kids + husband to get vasectomy soon + no other abnormalities; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: endometrial ablation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 11F + Tanner stage 3 breast and pubic hair; these findings are most predictive of what?
rapidFireQAs.a: “menarche is imminent.” USMLE wants you to know that menarche is imminent once girl is Tanner stage 3. Normal sequence is adrenarche → thelarche → pubarche → menarche.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13F + Tanner stage 2 + never had menstruation + brought in by mom concerned about lack of menstruation
rapidFireQAs.a: follow-up in 6 months (Tanner stage 2 so menarche is not yet imminent).

rapidFireQAs.q: 14F + 4x6cm mass in left breast + slightly tender + vitals normal + aunt died of breast cancer; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: follow-up in 6 months → virginal breast hypertrophy is normal response to increased estrogens in adolescence (also seen in males; asked on peds and FM shelves).

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + 10 weeks’ gestation + nausea and vomiting for 4 weeks + lost 1.8kg; what is the most likely adverse effect on the fetus?
rapidFireQAs.a: “no significant adverse effect.”

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)?
rapidFireQAs.a: urinary ketones.

rapidFireQAs.q: When does HG present + what’s the mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: 8-10 weeks’ gestation; an effect of beta-hCG (levels are highest at 8-10 weeks).

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in HG?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemic, hypochloremic, metabolic alkalosis (low K, low Cl, high bicarb); yes, they ask this on Obgyn shelf.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for HG?
rapidFireQAs.a: admit to hospital and give parenteral anti-emetic therapy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important drug causing hyperprolactinemia apart from antipsychotics?
rapidFireQAs.a: metoclopramide → D2 antagonist.

rapidFireQAs.q: Amenorrhea in patient with anorexia; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased GnRH pulsation (hypogonadotropic) → decreased LH + FSH; Q wants “↓ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer; in contrast, premature ovarian failure, Turner syndrome, and menopause have “↑ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + tight-fitting sports bra and/or breast trauma; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fat necrosis (can calcify).

rapidFireQAs.q: 36F + rubbery, mobile, painless mass in breast; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fibroadenoma → first Dx with USS only if age <30; do USS +/- mammogram if age >30; do FNA next; if confirmed, Tx = surgical excision; should be noted that guidelines vary (i.e., observe for change, etc.), but excision is definitive. Obgyn shelf will only ask you for Dx based on presentation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mammogram guidelines?
rapidFireQAs.a: start age 50 + every two years until age 75.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + painless unilateral cyst in breast that drains brown serous fluid; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Surg form 6 = fibrocystic change; everyone is surprised because, yes, classic presentation is bilateral breast tenderness in woman 20s-40s that waxes and wanes with menstrual cycle; Tx is supportive (Evening Primrose oil / warm bath); histological descriptors can be: sclerosing adenosis; blue dome cysts; apocrine metaplasia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + sharp pain in outer quadrant of right breast + exam shows 2cm tender area in right breast but no mass found; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fibrocystic change.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47F + breast lump self-palpated + breast USS shows 3cm complex cyst + FNA performed of the cyst revealing straw-colored fluid + mass still present after aspiration; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: biopsy of the mass.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + unilateral rusty nipple discharge; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + unilateral rusty nipple discharge + biopsy shows stellate morphology; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: invasive ductal carcinoma, not intraductal papilloma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + mammography shows cluster of microcalcifications in upper-outer quadrant; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: needle-guided open biopsy (FNA wrong answer) → microcalcifications are ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) until proven otherwise.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + inverted nipple + greenish discharge; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mammary ductal ectasia (widening of lactiferous duct).

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + recurrent miscarriage + SLE; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant) → Obgyn shelf will ask for “uteroplacental insufficiency” as the answer → Tx with aspirin or heparin; warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy (bone abnormalities + bleeding in fetus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + SLE + commencing third course of corticosteroids during past 18 months; Q asks what else she should be given
rapidFireQAs.a: “alendronate now” → give bisphosphonate to patients commencing steroids indefinitely, or to patients receiving steroids frequently.

rapidFireQAs.q: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) of the fetus; which lifestyle factor most contributory
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking, not alcohol → causes decreased placental blood flow → answer = “Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Which fetal parameter most reflective of IUGR?
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal circumference; sounds wrong, as you’d expect perhaps femur length, or biparietal diameter, etc., but answer is abdominal circumference.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + 33 weeks’ gestation + FVL mutation + intrauterine female demise; Q asks which vessel the thrombosis most likely occurred in
rapidFireQAs.a: uteroplacental artery.

rapidFireQAs.q: Female at 24 weeks’ gestation + HTN + proteinuria; most likely cause for her findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: “uteroplacental insufficiency” or “placental dysfunction”; this is the cause of preeclampsia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Female at 16 weeks’ gestation + HTN + proteinuria + fundal height measured at the umbilicus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hydatidiform mole, not preeclampsia; preeclampsia will occur after 20 weeks’ gestation; molar pregnancy presents large for gestational age → fundal height at umbilicus is normally reflective of 20 weeks’ gestation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Uteroplacental insufficiency can cause what issue on the fetal heart tracing?
rapidFireQAs.a: late decelerations (fetal hypoxia).

rapidFireQAs.q: What do early, variable, and late decels mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: early = fetal head compression; variable = cord compression; late = fetal hypoxia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fetus has HR at 120bpm (NR 110-160), however there’s zero variability; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = fetal sleep state.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fetus has HR at 180bpm, however there’s zero variability; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = maternal fever.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are accelerations?
rapidFireQAs.a: fetal well-being → rise of ~20bpm lasting ~20 seconds; 2-3 occurences every 20 minutes.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is a biophysical profile?
rapidFireQAs.a: assesses fetal wellbeing; often done when non-stress test (checking for accelerations) is non-reactive; five components of biophysical profile (you do not need to have these memorized for the USMLE; more just be aware that if the vignette mentions qualitative non-reassurance of any aspect of the biophysical profile, then there is possibly fetal/maternal pathology): Non-stress test shows at least two accelerations in 20 minutes. Rhythmic breathing episode of >30 seconds in 20 minutes. Fetal movements (at least 2 or 3 of the limbs). Fetal muscle tone (at least one episode of flexion/extension of the trunk + limbs together). Amniotic fluid volume (at least 2cm in vertical axis, or fluid index >5cm).

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + 41 weeks’ gestation + 4cm dilated + variable decels; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obygn NBME = amnioinfusion (wrong answers were external cephalic version, forceps delivery, amniocentesis, cordocentesis) → can’t attempt delivery if not 10cm dilated + forceps not tried first anyway because it can cause nerve damage or sternocleidomastoid trauma (vacuum extraction / suction cup delivery first).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is external cephalic version?
rapidFireQAs.a: transabdominal manipulation of a breech fetus into cephalic engagement; only performed after 36 weeks, as the fetus can spontaneously engage cephalically prior.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is internal podalic version?
rapidFireQAs.a: reorienting fetus within the womb during a breech delivery; may be attempted for transverse and oblique lies when C-section not performed; also used for delivery of second twins. I’ve never seen this as correct answer on NBME assessment; it just shows up a lot as an incorrect answer choice, so I’m mentioning it here because students always ask, “what’s that?”

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-day-old neonate + purplish fluctuant mound on scalp + crosses suture lines; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: caput succedaneum

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between caput succedaneum and cephalohematoma?
rapidFireQAs.a: Caput succedaneum is poorly defined soft tissue edema on the scalp; caused by pressure of fetal scalp against cervix during parturition, leading to transient decreased blood flow and reactive edema; crosses suture lines; can be purplish in color similar to cephalohematoma (i.e., don’t use color to distinguish); complications rare; disappears in hours to few days. Cephalohematoma is well-defined, localized, fluctuant swelling; caused by subperiosteal hemorrhage; does not cross suture lines; may be associated with underlying skull fracture, clotting disorders, jaundice; disappears in weeks to months. Caput succedaneum is poorly defined soft tissue edema on the scalp; caused by pressure of fetal scalp against cervix during parturition, leading to transient decreased blood flow and reactive edema; crosses suture lines; can be purplish in color similar to cephalohematoma (i.e., don’t use color to distinguish); complications rare; disappears in hours to few days. Cephalohematoma is well-defined, localized, fluctuant swelling; caused by subperiosteal hemorrhage; does not cross suture lines; may be associated with underlying skull fracture, clotting disorders, jaundice; disappears in weeks to months.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + G1P0 + third trimester + itchy hives-like eruptions within abdominal striae; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP); occurs in ~1/200 pregnancies (usually primigravid); cause is unknown, presents as pruritic hives-like eruption within striae; Tx is with topical emollients; for severe cases, topical steroids can be given; resolves spontaneously within a week of delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + G1P0 + third trimester + itchy palms + soles; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP); usually occurs third trimester; pruritis, particularly of palms + soles; diagnosis is achieved by ordering serum bile acids (elevated); Tx = ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol); important to note that ICP is associated with increased risk of third-trimester spontaneous abortion – i.e., it is not benign; delivery at 35-37 weeks may be considered; if bile acid levels normal, new literature suggests waiting until 39 weeks is acceptable.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + 30 weeks’ gestation + 10-day Hx of nausea and generalized itching + bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL + ALT/AST/ALP all normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn shelf answer = intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; no mention of palms + soles itching in vignette.

rapidFireQAs.q: 36F + G1P0 + 36 weeks’ gestation + nausea/vomiting + jaundice + high bilirubin + high ALT and AST + no mention of pruritis of palms/soles; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute fatty liver of pregnancy; caused by deficiency of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (sounds absurdly pedantic but asked on Obgyn shelf); often fatal; Tx is IV hydration + hepatology/high-risk obgyn consults + delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + G1P0 + 2nd or 3rd trimester + intensily itchy eruption around umbilicus that spreads outward; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: herpes gestationis (gestational pemphigoid); not HSV, but instead an idiopathic autoimmune phenomenon; Tx = topical steroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13F + never had menstrual period + morning nausea/vomiting + suprapubic fullness; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: beta-hCG → can get pregnant before first menstruation; Q also on peds NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for preeclampsia?
rapidFireQAs.a: HTN Mx (labetalol, methyldopa, etc.); definitive Tx is delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for eclampsia?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mg for seizures; definitive is delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for HTN emergencies in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: just know hydralazine can be used for this purpose.

rapidFireQAs.q: Female at 8 weeks’ gestation + cysts visualized bilaterally on pelvic USS; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: theca-lutein cysts → benign finding in pregnancy + will almost always naturally regress → increased occurrence in high beta-hCG states like multiple gestation pregnancy, moles, choriocarcinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: Complete vs partial mole?
rapidFireQAs.a: complete mole = karyotype of 46; empty egg fertilized by a sperm that duplicates; bunches of grapes / snowstorm appearance on USS; chance of progression to choriocarcinoma higher than partial; partial mole = karyotype of 69; fetal parts visible on USS; lesser chance of progression to choriocarcinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: Anovulation + hirsutism + BMI 27; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: PCOS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Anovulation; mechanism USMLE wants?
rapidFireQAs.a: insulin resistance → causes abnormal GnRH pulsation → high LH/FSH → LH high enough to precipitate ovulation but follicle not yet adequately primed → no ovulation (anovulation) → follicle retained as cyst.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why hirsutism in anovulation
rapidFireQAs.a: higher relative LH → more androgen production by theca interna cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: Best Tx for PCOS?
rapidFireQAs.a: if high BMI, weight loss first always on USMLE; if they ask for meds and/or weight loss already tried? → OCPs (if not wanting pregnancy); clomiphene (if wanting pregnancy; estrogen receptor partial agonist → leads to increased GnRH outflow).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + unable to conceive for 3 years + BMI 30 + acanthosis nigricans; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: T2DM (PCOS or anovulation not listed as answers; wrong answer is “hypercortisolism”) → Q doesn’t mention any characteristic features such as purple striae, muscle wasting, or central obesity.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40F + vasomotor Sx; which hormone to confirm Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: high FSH for premature ovarian failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + Hashimoto thyroiditis + hot flashes for 6 months + high FSH; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “autoimmune ovarian failure”; this is a cause of premature ovarian failure (autoimmune diseases go together).

rapidFireQAs.q: Thyroid and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: TSH normal, T3 normal, free T4 normal, total T4 elevated → due to increased thyroid-binding globulin due to higher estrogen.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do we order to evaluate thyroid function in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: always choose free T4 if you are asked. TSH is for screening in non-pregnant persons. Free T4 can be an answer in non-pregnant persons if they ask for most definitive marker for thyroid function.

rapidFireQAs.q: Levothyroxine dose in pregnancy for those with Hashimoto?
rapidFireQAs.a: may need to be increased up to 50%.

rapidFireQAs.q: Thionamides in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: methimazole is teratogenic in first trimester (causes aplasia cutis congenita); give PTU in first trimester; 2nd trimester onward switch to methimazole (PTU significantly hepatotoxic + methimazole only teratogenic early in pregnancy).

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + 34 weeks’ gestation + thyroid storm; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn NBME answer = PTU.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + gave birth to healthy boy 6 months ago following uncomplicated labor + no weight change or mood disturbance + on no meds + vitals WNL + dry skin + thyroid gland enlarged and non-tender + TSH high + T4 low; most likely explanation for these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: “thyroiditis” → Dx = postpartum thyroiditis (a type of silent thyroiditis) → characterized by thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism (1/3 of women experience both phases; 1/3 experience just hyperthyroid phase; 1/3 only hypothyroid phase); affects 5-10% of women postpartum; hyperthyroid phase usually occurs 1-4 months postpartum; hypothyroid phase occurs about 4-8 months postpartum; thought to be caused by postpartum immunologic rebound (immune system normally suppressed during pregnancy); Dx w/ Hx + ordering serum TSH; increased risk of progression to Hashimoto; Tx w/ short course of propranolol if hyperthyroid; give short course of levothyroxine if hypothyroid.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born with cretinism; what could have prevented this?
rapidFireQAs.a: “routine newborn screening”; yes, on obgyn shelf.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + anterior vaginal wall pain and dysuria for 6 months + U/A normal + vitals normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic interstitial cystitis → Tx is supportive; do not choose steroids.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important factoids about acute appendicitis in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: can be upper right quadrant; if appendicitis, yes, perform laparascopic appendectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Beta-hCG in mole vs ectopic?
rapidFireQAs.a: super-high in mole; low in ectopic (and slow rate of increase).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + presentation similar to stroke + beta-hCG hundreds of thousands; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: choriocarcinoma (brain mets); chorio loves to metastasize to lungs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + pregnancy visualized in the corneum of the uterus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ectopic pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + pregnancy visualized in the parametrium of the uterus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ectopic pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common location for ectopic?
rapidFireQAs.a: ampulla of fallopian tubes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common etiology for ectopic?
rapidFireQAs.a: Hx of PID → scarring of fallopian tubes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for ectopic pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: laparoscopic removal (salpingostomy / salpingectomy).

rapidFireQAs.q: When to give methotrexate to Tx ectopic?
rapidFireQAs.a: all must be fulfilled: beta-hCG <6,000; < 3 cm in size; fetal HR not detectable; no evidence of fluid leakage in the cul de sac; mom stable vitals.

rapidFireQAs.q: Organisms causing PID + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chlamydia and/or gonorrhea; Tx = IM ceftriaxone, PLUS either oral azithromycin or oral doxycycline. If patient is septic (2+ SIRS), answer = admit to hospital and give IV antibiotic therapy (they make this distinction on Obgyn shelf).

rapidFireQAs.q: PID + fever does not improve after several days on Abx; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: adnexal USS to look for tubo-ovarian abscess → must drain if present.

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between inevitable and threatened abortions?
rapidFireQAs.a: inevitable = bleeding + open cervix; threatened = bleeding + closed cervix; Tx for inevitable = vacuum aspiration; Tx for threatened = bed rest.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + 9 weeks’ gestation + bleeding and passage of clots per vaginum + intrauterine pregnancy seen on USS; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: incomplete abortion (passage of clots means it’s already underway).

rapidFireQAs.q: Difference between complete and missed abortions?
rapidFireQAs.a: Complete = no products of conception seen on USS (abortion is literally over/complete); missed = fetal demise without passage of products of conception.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + vaginal bleeding at 6 weeks’ gestation and beta-hCG 450 mIU/mL + USS shows thickened endometrial stripe and no fetal pole + one week later beta-hCG is 90 mIU/mL; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “third measurement of beta-hCG within one week” → Dx here is spontaneous abortion; must measure beta-hCG weekly until negative; same for gestational trophoblastic disease (moles).

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + bleeding per vaginum + uterus is large and smooth; Q asks for which type of uterine fibroid
rapidFireQAs.a: submucosal leiomyomata.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + no bleeding per vaginum + uterus is globular; which type of fibroid?
rapidFireQAs.a: subserosal.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + beefy red mass protruding from the vagina; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pedunculated submucosal leiomyomata uteri, not cervical cancer → the latter will often be described as an ulcerated, exophytic mass.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + comes in for routine exam + no complaints + large uterus on exam + USS shows various leiomyomata; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: observation (because asymptomatic); otherwise Tx = NSAIDs, OCPs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44F + dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia + USS shows large, smooth uterus with no overt masses; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: adenomyosis (endometrium growing within myometrium); may present similar to submucosal fibroids, with vaginal bleeding, however uterus is diffusely enlarged and no masses seen on USS; Tx with NSAIDs, OCPs; leuprolide; definitive is hysterectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + 30 weeks’ gestation + weakness of thumb abduction bilaterally; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: carpal tunnel syndrome (normal in pregnancy).

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + unintended pregnancy + fever of 104F + vaginal discharge + abdo pain + laceration visualized on cervix; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: septic abortion → she tried to self-abort using, e.g., a hanger.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + rupture of membranes (ROM) >18 hours + abdo pain + fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chorioamnionitis; Tx = ampicillin + gentamicin + clindamycin (amp + gent alone seen as answer on one Obgyn shelf Q).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + C-section 12 hours ago + abdo pain + fever; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: postpartum endometritis; Tx = ampicillin + gentamicin + clindamycin.

rapidFireQAs.q: Organism(s) causing chorioamnionitis + endometritis?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymicrobial.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + postpartum endometritis + low BP; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: puerperal sepsis; gynecologic infection starting 1-10 days after parturition leading to sepsis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Lump seen at 4 or 8 o’clock position on vulva; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Bartholin gland cyst/abscess; Tx = warm compresses for cyst; drain if abscess.

rapidFireQAs.q: Organism(s) causing Bartholin gland abscess?
rapidFireQAs.a: polymicrobial.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + Bartholin gland abscess + Q asks “most serious complication of this condition?”
rapidFireQAs.a: necrotizing fasciitis; wrong answer = “gram positive sepsis” (polymicrobial; need not be gram +).

rapidFireQAs.q: Grey/whitish patchy/rough area on the vulva or perineum; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: lichen sclerosus → must do punch biopsy first to rule out SCC; if confirmed LS, do topical steroids; if SCC, surgically excise.

rapidFireQAs.q: SCC of perineum in diabetic; biggest risk factor in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: HPV, not dysglycemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + sharp adnexal pain + no adnexal mass mentioned in vignette + 10-15 mL of serosanguinous fluid aspirated from the cul de sac; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ruptured cyst (usually corpus luteal); Tx = supportive.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + Hx of ovarian cyst + colicky pelvic pain past few weeks + pain has become constant past couple days + 6x8cm palpable adnexal mass; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ovarian/adnexal torsion (cyst is a risk factor).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + Hx of ovarian cyst + intermittent pelvic pain for four hours that has become constant past two hours + 8x10cm palpable adnexal mass; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ovarian/adnexal torsion (pain may be weeks or hours).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + increasingly severe pelvic pain the past couple days + 6x8cm mass palpable in the adnexa; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: torsion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + normal periods + LMP 20 days ago + 5cm mobile mass in right adnexa on examination + slightly tender to palpation; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst; wrong answer is endometrioma (chocolate cyst seen in endometriosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + tampon use + diffuse rash + BP 90/60; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: toxic shock syndrome (S.aureus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + 30 weeks’ gestation + spotting on underwear 12 hours after sexual intercourse + bleeding gradually increasing since + USS normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical trauma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 36F + 26 weeks’ gestation + severe flank pain + feels faint when attempting to urinate; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: urolithiasis (progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for increased cholesterol gallstones in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: progesterone slows biliary peristalsis + estrogen increased activity of HMG-CoA reductase (compensatory for lowering serum levels of cholesterol).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + three first-trimester miscarriages + has single kidney; Q asks most likely reason for recurrent miscarriage
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital uterine abnormalities.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for torsion?
rapidFireQAs.a: laparoscopic detorsion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + dull right-sided pelvic pain + beta-hCG negative + USS shows simple 5cm cyst; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “oral contraceptive therapy and a second pelvic examination in 6 weeks”; the wrong answer is “reassurance and schedule follow-up examination in 1 year.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + extremely painful periods + needs to miss grad school classes sometimes because of the pain + examination shows no abnormalities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary dysmenorrhea = “prostaglandin production” = PGF2alpha hypersecretion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Above 23F; next best step in Mx?
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAIDs; pregnancy test is wrong answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + extremely painful periods + needs to miss grad school classes sometimes because of the pain + examination shows nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: endometriosis. Obgyn shelf will often omit details such as pain with defecation or dyspareunia because they’re too easy.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx endometriosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: diagnostic laparoscopy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + dull pelvic pain + USS shows cystic mass with calcification; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma); details such as “hair, skin, teeth” are too easy for Obgyn shelf.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65F + multiple masses “caked” on the omentum; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ovarian cancer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F with epilepsy + 10 weeks’ gestation + has seizure + phenytoin serum level below therapeutic range; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: increase dose of phenytoin (yes, during pregnancy) → seizure leads to fetal hypoxia, which is worse case scenario, so must prevent at all costs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F on valproic acid wanting to get pregnant; what do we do?
rapidFireQAs.a: stop valproic acid (contraindicated in pregnancy due to high chance of neural tube defects) → can use other anti-epileptics during pregnancy instead.

rapidFireQAs.q: Hx of many pregnancies + downward movement of vesicourethral junction
rapidFireQAs.a: stress incontinence → answer on one Obgyn NBME Q is “decreased external urethral tone.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Hyperactive detrusor or detrusor instability
rapidFireQAs.a: urge incontinence.

rapidFireQAs.q: Need to run to bathroom when sticking key in a door
rapidFireQAs.a: urge incontinence.

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence in multiple sclerosis patient or perimenopausal
rapidFireQAs.a: urge incontinence.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + hot flashes + urge incontinence; Q asks mechanism
rapidFireQAs.a: “estrogen deficiency.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of urge incontinence
rapidFireQAs.a: oxybutynin (muscarinic cholinergic antagonist) or mirabegron (beta-3 agonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence + high post-void volume (usually 3-400 in question; normal is <50 mL)
rapidFireQAs.a: overflow incontinence.

rapidFireQAs.q: Incontinence in diabetes
rapidFireQAs.a: overflow incontinence due to neurogenic bladder.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for overflow incontinence in diabetes
rapidFireQAs.a: bethanechol (muscarinic cholinergic agonist).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the only approved indication for hormone-replacement therapy (HRT)?
rapidFireQAs.a: severe vasomotor Sx (hot flushes, urge incontinence); HRT is not used for preserving bone density; increases risk of thromboembolic and cerebrovascular events; estrogen increases fibrinogen and factor VIII levels.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57F + blood stains on underwear for 6 months + painful sexual intercourse + atrophic, friable vaginal mucosa on exam + cervix and bimanual exams normal; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: atrophic vaginitis → answer = “hypoestrogenic state” → Tx = lubricants; if insufficient, topical estrogen may be used.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + currently breastfeeding + menstruation not yet resumed + dyspareunia + erythematous vagina with no discharge; next best step in Mx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “recommendation for use of a lubricant” → high prolactin levels during breastfeeding → hypoestrogenic state → Sx similar to atrophic vaginitis in menopause.

rapidFireQAs.q: HRT increases the risk of what kind of cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: breast, not endometrial; greater absolute amount of estrogen over female’s life increases breast cancer risk; HRT does not increase endometrial cancer risk; latter is unopposed estrogen as risk factor, which is why HRT is estrogen + progesterone; only time HRT is given as estrogen only is for women with Hx of hysterectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 53F + taking HRT past six months + stopped taking progesterone component because she didn’t like how it affected her moods + vaginal bleeding; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn shelf = endometrial biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 53F + started HRT three months ago + normal mammogram when started HRT + now has cyst seen on ultrasound after self-palpation; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: FNA biopsy of the cyst.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do combined oral contraceptive pills affect cancer risk:
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓↓ ovarian (~50% ↓ risk), ↓ endometrial, ↔ breast; ↑ cervical (from decreased barrier protection → ↑ HPV infections; not from pill itself). Some studies have suggested possible increased risk for breast, but no significance.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + aunt died of ovarian cancer + asks GP how to screen for ovarian cancer; what is your response?
rapidFireQAs.a: no screening, but offer her information about oral contraceptive pills.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + BRCA mutation confirmed + three first-degree family members with gynecologic cancers; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47F + total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy performed for leiomyomata uteri; Q asks what we do re Pap smears
rapidFireQAs.a: “no longer indicated.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + T1DM + 33 weeks’ gestation + fundal height 38cm; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: polyhydramnios (fundal height in cm should approximately = # of weeks pregnant).

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonatal girl with karyotype 46XX + has phallus and scrotum; Q asks mechanism
rapidFireQAs.a: “ACTH hypersecretion” → in congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 21- and 11-hydroxylase deficiency, cortisol is low, so ACTH goes up to compensate, leading to cortical hyperplasia; in addition, precursors are shunted to DHEA-S and androstenedione, leading virilization of newborn.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + prenatal USS shows two fetuses with thick dividing membrane; what kind of twin pregnancy is this?
rapidFireQAs.a: dichorionic diamniotic; thick dividing membrane = two chorions; # of placentae = # of chorions.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + prenatal USS shows one fetus much larger than the other; what kind of twin pregnancy is this?
rapidFireQAs.a: most likely to be monochorionic monoamnionic in the setting of twin-twin transfusion syndrome, where one fetus “steals”/siphons nutrients and blood flow from his or her twin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + receiving beta-hCG as part of IVF protocol + develops severe abdo pain + ascites; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome → almost always due to iatrogenic beta-hCG administration; causes vascular hyperpermeability.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + requests OCPs + Pap smear is normal; Q asks what else needs to be done
rapidFireQAs.a: check for chlamydia → should be noted that whilst Pap smears always start at 21, STI checks are done from age of sexual onset.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + regular periods + Hx of multiple sexual partners + unable to conceive with husband for 3 years + husband has normal semen sample; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: hysterosalpingogram (assess tubal patency and uterine architecture; possible Hx of PID leading to tubal occlusion (despite no Hx of ectopic in the patient).

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + hysterosalpingogram shows spillage of dye into the peritoneal cavity; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal finding (fallopian tubes are normally open at both ends).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is uterine didelphys?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterus develops as paired organ (double uterus) + double cervix +/- double vagina.

rapidFireQAs.q: 52F + presents for routine screening for first time in 4 years; Q asks in addition to cholesterol screening, Pap smear, and mammography; what does she need?
rapidFireQAs.a: colonoscopy. Similar answers might be influenza vaccine if fall/winter (every year).

rapidFireQAs.q: How often are Pap smears indicated, and when are they started and stopped?
rapidFireQAs.a: commenced at age 21, then every 3 years; starting age 30, can become every 5 years if co-test for HPV; performed until age 65 (past ten years must be normal findings + no Hx of moderate or severe dysplasia).

rapidFireQAs.q: Pap smears in HIV?
rapidFireQAs.a: at time of diagnosis, then every year.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mx of Pap smear result: atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US)
rapidFireQAs.a: repeat cytology in a year, OR test for HPV; if positive, do colposcopy + biopsy; if negative, repeat co-testing in three years.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mx of LSIL on Pap smear?
rapidFireQAs.a: if negative HPV testing, repeat co-testing in one year; if (+) HPV testing or no testing, do colposcopy + biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mx of high-grade squamous intraepithelial neoplasia (HSIL) on Pap smear?
rapidFireQAs.a: regardless of HPV status: immediate loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), OR colposcopy + biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mx of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) I seen on biopsy
rapidFireQAs.a: immediate LEEP, OR colposcopy + cytology every 6 months.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mx of CIN II/III seen on biopsy
rapidFireQAs.a: immediate LEEP demonstrating clear margins, then do Pap + HPV contesting 1 and 2 years postoperatively.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57F + vaginal hysterectomy performed for CIN III; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn shelf answer = “Pap smear annually.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + colposcopy is performed for LSIL + entire squamocolumnar junction cannot be visualized; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = cone biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47F + Pap smear shows atypical glandular cells + colposcopy normal + endocervical curettage shows benign cells; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn NBME answer = endometrial biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + two minutes after separation of placenta has shortness of breath + tachycardia + bleeding from venipuncture sites; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: amniotic fluid embolism; can cause DIC; supportive care.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + two days after C-section + gets up to go to the bathroom + SoB + tachycardia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary embolism → heparin followed by spiral CT (if not pregnant) or V/Q scan (if pregnant).

rapidFireQAs.q: 39F + pregnant + Sx of pulmonary embolism + V/Q scan performed showing segmental defects; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: spiral CT; student says “wait but I thought we don’t do CT in pregnancy.” Right, we don’t. But if they ask for next best step after V/Q scan, that’s still the answer they want.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + two days after C-section + temp 100.8F + breath sounds decreased at both lung bases + urinary catheter specimen is negative + remainder of exam unremarkable; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: atelectasis (most common cause of fever within 24 hours of surgery (but shelf has two days after C-section for one Q).

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + triad of third-trimester painless bleeding + ROM + fetal bradycardia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: vasa previa (fetal vessels overlying the internal cervical os); associated with velamentous cord insertion (vessels not protected by Wharton jelly).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + uncomplicated delivery of newborn + heavy vaginal bleeding + placenta shows large, non-tapering vessel extending to margin of membranes; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: succenturiate placental lobe; students is surprised? → just need to know sometimes placenta can have auxiliary lobe with connecting vessels; this is a cause of vasa previa, in addition to velamentous cord insertion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + C-section 6 weeks ago + required 3 units of transfused RBCs + 9kg weight loss + has cold intolerance + could not breastfeed; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Sheehan syndrome (arrow Q on shelf; answer is ↓ for prolactin, ACTH, GH, FSH, TSH); should be noted tangentially that on newer NBME for Step 1, Q with Sheehan syndrome has ↑ for aldosterone (not hyperaldosteronism, but higher baseline to compensate for lower cortisol).

rapidFireQAs.q: 15F + never had menstrual period + one-wk Hx of constant, severe pelvic pain + 10-month Hx of intermittent pelvic pain + BP of 90/50 + bluish bulge in upper vagina; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hematometra → imperforate hymen with blood collection in the uterus → vagal response causes low BP → Tx = cruciate incision of the hymen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 15F + never had menstrual period + one-wk Hx of constant, severe pelvic pain + 10-month Hx of intermittent pelvic pain + BP normal + bluish bulge in upper vagina; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hematocolpos → blood collection in the vaginal canal, but not backed up to the uterus like hematometra → Tx = cruciate incision of the hymen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + delivered newborn 5 days ago + pain in calf with dorsiflexion of foot; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: duplex ultrasonography of the calf; positive Homan sign for DVT in hypercoagulable state.

rapidFireQAs.q: Down syndrome important testing?
rapidFireQAs.a: First trimester screen (11-13 weeks): ↓ pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPPA), ↑ beta-hCG, ↑ nuchal translucency, hypoplastic nasal bone. Second trimester screen (16-18 weeks): ↓ AFP, ↑ beta-hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin-A; in Edward syndrome, all decreased; Patau is variable. Cell-free DNA (as early as 10 weeks). First trimester screen (11-13 weeks): ↓ pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPPA), ↑ beta-hCG, ↑ nuchal translucency, hypoplastic nasal bone. Second trimester screen (16-18 weeks): ↓ AFP, ↑ beta-hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin-A; in Edward syndrome, all decreased; Patau is variable. Cell-free DNA (as early as 10 weeks).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of abnormal AFP measurement?
rapidFireQAs.a: dating error.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + AFP measurement comes back 2.6x upper limit of normal; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: re-ultrasound; wrong answer = perform AFP measurement again → need to simply do ultrasound to reapproximate dates.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important locations for the “celes”:
rapidFireQAs.a: Cystocele: anterior superior vaginal wall. Urethrocele: anterior inferior vaginal wall. Enterocele: posterior superior vaginal wall (Q on shelf says “high on posterior vaginal wall; another Q says the patient can feel movement within her vagina → weird, but presumably gut peristalsis). Rectocele: posterior inferior vaginal wall. Cystocele: anterior superior vaginal wall. Urethrocele: anterior inferior vaginal wall. Enterocele: posterior superior vaginal wall (Q on shelf says “high on posterior vaginal wall; another Q says the patient can feel movement within her vagina → weird, but presumably gut peristalsis). Rectocele: posterior inferior vaginal wall.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + protrusion of distal urethra through urethral meatus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: urethral prolapse; sounds reasonable, but don’t confuse with stress incontinence; the latter will sometimes be described as “downward mobility of vesicourethral junction with Valsalva” (not urethral prolapse).

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + 24 weeks’ gestation + fundal height 20cm + no cervix palpated + examination shows fetus in breech position in vagina; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical incompetence; Tx w/ cervical cerclage; notable risk factor is prior conization.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + 37 weeks’ gestation + fetus in breech position; during labor, risk of which complication is greatest?
rapidFireQAs.a: cord prolapse.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + 14 weeks’ gestation + Hx of two LEEP + cervix flush against upper vagina and measures 2cm in diameter + pelvic USS shows funneled lower uterine segment; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical incompetence → “funnel” means cervical incompetence (“cervical funneling” / “funneled lower uterine segment”).

rapidFireQAs.q: 87F + partial prolapse of uterine cervix through the introitus + uterus can easily be pushed back into the uterus; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: vaginal pessary.

rapidFireQAs.q: Stages of labor:
rapidFireQAs.a: Stage 1 latent: 0-6cm cervical dilation (old guidelines: 0-4cm). Stage 1 active: 6-10cm (complete) cervical dilation. (old guidelines: 4-10cm). Stage 2: 10cm (complete) cervical dilation to delivery of fetus. Stage 3: delivery of fetus to delivery of placenta. Obgyn NBME has Q where 32F has been at 5cm dilation for past 4 hours; answer = “arrest of active phase”; the wrong answer is “protracted latent phase.” Stage 1 latent: 0-6cm cervical dilation (old guidelines: 0-4cm). Stage 1 active: 6-10cm (complete) cervical dilation. (old guidelines: 4-10cm). Stage 2: 10cm (complete) cervical dilation to delivery of fetus. Stage 3: delivery of fetus to delivery of placenta. Obgyn NBME has Q where 32F has been at 5cm dilation for past 4 hours; answer = “arrest of active phase”; the wrong answer is “protracted latent phase.”

rapidFireQAs.q: What is definition of protracted latent phase?
rapidFireQAs.a: dilating <1-2cm per hour, which reflects the 95%tile in contemporary women. Women <6cm are in latent phase; regardless of parity, may take 6-7 hours to progress from 4-5cm, and 3-4 hours to progress from 5-6cm.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does “arrest of active phase” mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: no cervical change in >4 hours despite adequate contractions (>200 Montevideo unites [MVU]), or >6 hours if contractions inadequate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + 38 weeks’ gestation + cervix completely dilated + strong contractions + fetal station remains unchanged over next hour; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cephalopelvic disproportion (baby too big for pelvis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 5F + foul-smelling yellow vaginal discharge + blood spotting on underpants + no dysuria + mild vulvar erythema seen on exam; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: vaginal foreign body, not sexual abuse; presumably sexual abuse there would be lacerations or trauma seen on physical exam.

rapidFireQAs.q: 82F + Alzheimer + brought in by daughter for blood on underwear + 3cm vaginal laceration + erythematous, edematous perineal body; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: sexual assault.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + dysuria + bacteriuria + pyuria; Q asks how to decrease future episodes
rapidFireQAs.a: “voiding immediately after coitus.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + three UTIs over past year + Hx of UTIs being Tx successfully with TMP-SMX; Q asks for most appropriate med for daily UTI prophylaxis
rapidFireQAs.a: TMP-SMX; slightly unusual question, but it’s on the Obygn NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + dysuria + urinalysis shows 20-50 WBCs/hpf + one week of TMP-SMX does not improve Sx; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: urethral culture for chlamydia → if patient doesn’t improve with Tx of UTI, check for STIs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + 40 weeks’ gestation + epidural catheter placed + lidocaine and epinephrine injected + develops metallic taste in mouth; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “intravascular injection of anesthetic.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + 5 weeks post-delivery + insomnia + irritable + finds baby’s cry annoying and leaves him in crib crying for long periods of time; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “arrange for immediate psychiatric evaluation” → post-partum depression; Tx = sertraline (SSRI) and CBT; if mania, delusions, or hallucinations → post-partum psychosis; if more mild + within 7-10 days of delivery → post-partum blues.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + 42 weeks’ gestation + oligohydramnios + cervix long, closed, and posterior; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “administer a prostaglandin”; wrong answer is amnioinfusion (do for variable decelerations with ROM).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + pregnant + low serum iron and ferritin + microcytic anemia + proceeds to take iron for three weeks + three weeks later, iron and ferritin are normal but still has microcytic anemia; next best step in Mx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “hemoglobin electrophoresis”; Dx is thalassemia (alpha trait usually, as this is asymptomatic + picked up in pregnancy) → microcytic anemia non-responsive to iron supplementation; Hb electrophoresis will show presence of HbA2.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + 7 weeks’ gestation + started taking prenatal vitamin 3 weeks ago + microcytic anemia; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemoglobin electrophoresis; same as above, the implication is that the supplement contains iron + she is possibly non-responsive to it → thalassemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + African American + 7 weeks’ gestation + microcytic anemia + Hb electrophoresis shows 95% HbA1; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn shelf = iron deficiency anemia; thalassemia would show HbA2.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + pregnant + MCV 87 + Hb 10.5 g/dL; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: physiologic dilution of pregnancy → Hb drop to 10.5 g/dL is normal finding.

rapidFireQAs.q: What about platelets in pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: reduction normal; gestational thrombocytopenia is the Dx when level drops to <150,000 per uL.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24F + immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); Q asks the potential effect on the fetus
rapidFireQAs.a: “fetal platelet destruction”; maternal IgG against her own platelet GpIIb/IIIa can cross placenta, attacking the fetal platelets. This is on new Obgyn form.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + 42 weeks’ gestation + shoulder dystocia + neonate born with arm pronated, adducted, and internally rotated; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “injury to the 5th and 6th cervical nerve roots” (Erb-Duchenne palsy).

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of postpartum bleeding?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterine atony (hypocontractile uterus).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for uterine atony?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterine massage first, followed by oxytocin, then ergonovine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + postpartum bleeding despite uterine massage and oxytocin; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: ergonovine therapy (do not give in HTN).

rapidFireQAs.q: Diabetic mom giving birth + shoulder dystocia + McRoberts maneuver implemented; what is notable risk to the fetus here?
rapidFireQAs.a: clavicular fracture (anterior shoulder caught behind pubic symphysis → McRoberts maneuver is flexing mom’s hips + applying suprapubic pressure → clavicular fracture not uncommon).

rapidFireQAs.q: Diabetic mom giving birth + shoulder dystocia + McRoberts maneuver implemented + postpartum bleeding + uterus is firm on palpation; most likely cause of bleeding?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn shelf = vaginal laceration, not uterine atony.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + delivers term neonate + placenta delivers after gentle cord traction + now has moderate vaginal bleeding + HR 60 + BP 60/40 + IV saline doesn’t help + uterus cannot be palpated on physical exam; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterine inversion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Episiotomy performed posterior in the midline; what does the obstetrician cut into if he cuts too far?
rapidFireQAs.a: external anal sphincter.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + 40 weeks’ gestation + Hx of C-section + constant, sharp abdominal pain + maternal vitals all normal + fetal late decels + “Leopold maneuvers show fetal small parts above the fundus”; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterine rupture.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + 40 weeks’ gestation + oxytocin administered + robust contractions occurring every two minutes + abdo pain + hypotension + fetal head palpated in RUQ; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: uterine rupture.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are tachysystole and uterine hypertonus?
rapidFireQAs.a: tachysystole is >5 contractions every ten minutes; uterine hypertonus is a sustained contraction >2 minutes.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are Leopold maneuvers?
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal palpatory maneuvers used to determine the position and lie of the fetus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 62F + ovarian mass + bleeding per vaginum + endometrial biopsy shows atypical complex hyperplasia; Q asks for which ovarian cancer is the Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: granulosa cell tumor → unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → endometrial cancer risk.

rapidFireQAs.q: 47F + 9-month Hx of irregular periods where they occur at 2-3-month intervals + endometrial biopsy shows proliferative endometrium; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on shelf = “cyclic progestin therapy” → control irregular menses and prevent endometrial hyperplasia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + menometrorrhagia + LMP 2 weeks ago + periods 28-30-day intervals + just started taking OCPs for Tx; what is the most likely explanation for improvement in patient’s bleeding?
rapidFireQAs.a: “synchronization of endometrium.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + G3P2 + Rh negative + received RhoGAM both prior pregnancies + arrives now at first prenatal visit for third pregnancy; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn shelf answer = “indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test” → must see if she’s developed antibodies to Rh antigen.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + G1P0 + O+ blood type + fetus is A or B blood + goes on to develops pathologic jaundice postpartum; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemolytic disease of the newborn (ABO type) → mothers with O blood type will have fractional IgG (instead of IgM) against A and B antigens → cross placenta → fetal hemolysis → severity highly variable; Obgyn shelf will always give first pregnancy and an O+ mom so that student can’t accidentally get lucky with the Dx if he/she only knows about Rh type hemolytic disease of the newborn.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + G2P1 + Rh negative + fetus experiences hydrops; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh type) → presumably mother made antibodies against fetal Rh antigen from prior pregnancy following mixing of circulations.

rapidFireQAs.q: When to give RhoGAM?
rapidFireQAs.a: normally at 28 weeks’ gestation + again at parturition; also give for spontaneous or instrumental abortions + procedures (e.g., amniocentesis) + trauma/insults (e.g., abruptio placentae).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + G3P2 + Rh negative + all pregnancies with same male partner + indirect Coombs test positive for anti-Kell antigens at titer of 1:256; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “Kell typing of the father’s blood”; implication is mom is Kell negative but prior fetus(es) Kell positive; fetal blood must have entered maternal blood during prior pregnancy, however mom has no titers against Rh, just Kell, because RhoGAM was presumably given.

rapidFireQAs.q: Painful third-trimester bleeding following MVA or cocaine use; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: abruptio placentae.

rapidFireQAs.q: Painless third-trimester bleeding; Dx until proven otherwise?
rapidFireQAs.a: placenta previa → placental implantation site can spontaneously move off the internal os before 36 weeks, so don’t plan for Caesar before then.

rapidFireQAs.q: Postpartum hemorrhage due to placental issue; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: placenta accreta/increta/percreta.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + recently took Abx + red vaginal introitus and itching + cervical and vaginal discharge are normal + KOH prep and wet mount show no abnormalities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = vaginal candidiasis (thick white discharge is otherwise classic). Tx = topical nystatin or oral fluconazole.

rapidFireQAs.q: 67F + T2DM + vaginal candidiasis Tx with topical miconazole + doesn’t respond to Tx; Q asks why
rapidFireQAs.a: T2DM.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + mucopurulent discharge + no organisms grow; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chlamydia → oral azithromycin or doxycycline. Azithromycin is ideal because it’s one-off stat oral dose; doxy is BID for a week.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + mucopurulent discharge + gram negative diplococci; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: gonorrhea → cotreat for chlamydia → IM ceftriaxone + oral azithro, OR IM cefixime + oral azithro.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + erythematous cervix + yellow/green discharge + wet mount confirms Dx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: trichomoniasis (flagellated protozoa) → Tx = topical metronidazole for patient and partner.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + erythematous vaginal canal + thin, watery discharge + wet mount confirms Dx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella vaginalis) → met mount shows clue cells (squamous cells covered in bacteria) → Tx = topical metronidazole.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + thin, grey discharge + KOH prep Whiff test is performed yielding fishy odor; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bacterial vaginosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + VDRL positive at titer of 1:4 + physical exam shows no abnormalities + complains of no Sx + chlamydia and gonorrhea testing negative; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn shelf answer = fluorescent treponema antibody (syphilis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 19F + painless vulvar ulcer + rapid plasmin reagin negative + all other tests negative; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn NBME answer = repeat rapid plasma reagin (slightly unusual answer, but can sometimes be negative early in primary syphilis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + one-week Hx of 0.25-cm crusty, painless papule on the posterior fourchette; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: condylomata acuminata → HPV6+11.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + soft pink papillary lesions on labia minora and posterior fourchette; Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on obgyn NBME = podophyllum resin; student is surprised? → used to treat warts.

rapidFireQAs.q: Gardasil HPV vaccine protects against which types?
24F + recently went backpacking in Asia + painful vulvar crater + gram (-) rods cultured; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chancroid (haemophilus ducreyi); Tx with azithromycin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + G1P0 + exposed to child with chickenpox + never been vaccinated against VZV; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: administer VZV IVIG within 96 hours (to be most effective, but still advised up to 10 days post-exposure).

rapidFireQAs.q: When is VZV IVIG advised for neonates?
rapidFireQAs.a: maternal active lesions between 5 days prior to and 2 days post-delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born with patent ductus arteriosus; what Sx did the mom have while pregnant?
rapidFireQAs.a: arthritis, not rash; Dx is congenital rubella syndrome in the neonate (causes PDA).

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + 22 weeks’ gestation + develops low-grade fever and rash + fetus develops hydrops; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: maternal infection with parovirus B19.

rapidFireQAs.q: 21F + painful vesicles on vulva; do we give oral or topical acyclovir?
rapidFireQAs.a: HSV → always oral if asked.

rapidFireQAs.q: Herpes and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: acyclovir indicated to reduce chance of active lesions at time of labor; if active lesions or prodromal Sx present at parturition, C-section is indicated; acyclovir is safe during pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: HIV and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: most important USMLE point is HAART therapy during pregnancy is more important than not breastfeeding in terms of decreasing vertical transmission; sounds strange, as the virus is literally in breastmilk, but the answer is HAART therapy to decrease viral load is most important to prevent vertical transmission; in addition, administer zidovudine to mom prior to C-section, then zidovudine within 12 hours to neonate post-delivery (latter Q on peds NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: Hepatitis B and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: if mom HepB +, give both HBIG + vaccine within 12 hours of birth; if mom HepB negative, give just vaccine within 12 hours of birth; if mom status unknown, give vaccine within 12 hours of birth, and give HBIG within 7 days if mom’s test comes back + or remains unknown.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + 14 weeks’ gestation + not immune to HepB; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: vaccinate to HepB now.

rapidFireQAs.q: Influenza and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: safe to give IM killed vaccine during pregnancy (in fall or winter).

rapidFireQAs.q: MMR vaccine and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: vaccinate before pregnancy; do not give during pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: TB and pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx for latent and active TB, yes; for active, Tx with RIPE for 2 months, followed by RI for 7 more months (9 months total); if not pregnant, RI is only given for 4 more months.

rapidFireQAs.q: Breastfeeding and OCPs?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obgyn shelf wants you to know that estrogen-containing contraception decreases protein content of breastmilk; also linked to lower milk supply + shorter duration of breastfeeding; contraindicated < 6 weeks postpartum; if hormonal contraception used, progestin-only recommended.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to differentiate between androgen insensitivity syndrome and Mullerian (paramesonephric duct) agenesis?
rapidFireQAs.a: both phenotypically female teenagers with normal Tanner stage development; both have vagina that ends in blind pouch; the clinical difference is that in androgen insensitivity syndrome, they will say absent or sparse pubic and axillary hair; in Mullerian agenesis, the hair pattern will be normal, or they’ll even explicitly say “coarse” pubic and axillary hair. If androgen insensitivity syndrome suspected, next best step = karyotyping (46XY); Mullerian agenesis is 46XX.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16F + never had menstrual period + 5’9” + sparse pubic and axillary hair; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: AIS → pointing out that the Q will say “a 16-year-old girl comes in,” but karyotypically the patient is still a male.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12F + 1-year Hx of progressive hair growth and acne + 2-cm vaginal canal + significant clitoromegaly + posterior labioscrotal fusion + no cervix or palpable uterus; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency → “phallus at age 12” (i.e., penis at age 12, since surge of testosterone at puberty yields significant DHT production despite deficient enzyme); Obgyn shelf will merely ask for the karyotype here; answer = 46XY (i.e., male, even though stem will say “12-year-old girl”).

rapidFireQAs.q: 17F + never had menstrual period + high FSH + absent breast development + scant pubic hair; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: karyotyping (Turner syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 15F + Tanner stage 2 + 4’11” + bone age is equal to chronologic age
rapidFireQAs.a: karyotyping (Turner).

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + C-section two days ago + incision site erythematous + abdomen tender + vitals normal + two palpable lymph nodes in groin; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “normal postoperative course.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + vaginal bleeding + hydroureter; Q asks for what kind of cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: cervical SCC (impingement on the ureter).

rapidFireQAs.q: When are OCPs contraindicated?
rapidFireQAs.a: smokers over 35; migraine with aura; HTN (>160/100); current or past venous thromboemboli; thrombotic disorder (i.e., prothrombin mutation, FVL); cerebrovascular event; ischemic heart disease; current breast cancer; liver tumor; among others; Obgyn shelf will ask which is contraindicated, and the answer is “triphasic oral contraceptives” (same thing as OCP).

rapidFireQAs.q: 18F + menstrual cycles with 14-40-day intervals + beta-hCG negative; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “cyclic progesterone therapy” → means OCPs, but this is shelf wording.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is most effective form of emergency contraception?
rapidFireQAs.a: copper IUD; second-best is ulipristal (selective progesterone-receptor modulator; SPRM).

rapidFireQAs.q: 31F + copper IUD in place + pelvic exam shows enlarged uterus + USS shows 4cm fibroid; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “leave the IUD in place but inform the patient that the leiomyoma may cause heavier menses.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Important points about Depo vs Implanon?
rapidFireQAs.a: Depo is progestin injection that is effective for three months; it can cause decreased bone density; Implanon is a progestin implant contraceptive that is effective for three years; it is associated with erratic periods.

rapidFireQAs.q: Type of cancer patient is at increased risk for if commencing Depo?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on Obgyn shelf = breast.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important contraindication to IUD?
rapidFireQAs.a: active STI/PID or Hx of infection within past 3 months; current pregnancy (obvious); Hx of gynecologic malignancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + HTN managed with meds + often forgets to take meds + wants contraception; what is most appropriate recommendation?
rapidFireQAs.a: levonorgestrel IUD (for patients with poor pharmacologic adherence).

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + Hx of difficulty remembering to take daily meds + wants contraception + Tx for chlamydia three months ago; Q asks most appropriate form of contraception
rapidFireQAs.a: “Depo medroxyprogesterone”; IUD not ideal because of Hx of infection past three months.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F + Hx of breast cancer + paresthesias bilaterally in legs; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids first for possible spinal mets (decrease inflammation); then do MRI of spine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + G2P1 + 10 weeks’ gestation + prior pregnancy resulted in neonate of 4540 grams; Q asks what she’s at increased risk for during current pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: gestational diabetes.

rapidFireQAs.q: When to screen for gestational diabetes (GD) for normal risk women?
rapidFireQAs.a: 24-28 weeks’ gestation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F diabetic + 37-weeks’ gestation + delivers neonate with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) + macrosomia (>4000 grams); Q asks which hormone in the serum of the fetus is responsible
rapidFireQAs.a: insulin → inhibits surfactant production; should be noted that insulin does not cross the placenta; fetus produces more endogenous insulin with maternal diabetes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for NRDS?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased surfactant production → decreased lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio; lecithin is aka dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 37F + 33 weeks’ gestation + C-section scheduled in 12 hours + bolus of steroids given 12 hours ago; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: give bolus of steroids; two boluses of steroids must be given within 24 hours of delivery <34 weeks.

rapidFireQAs.q: When to give steroids and magnesium prior to delivery?
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids before 34 weeks (two boluses); if 34 0/7 – 36 6/7 weeks, give one bolus of steroids; add magnesium if before 32 weeks.

rapidFireQAs.q: When are tocolytics used?
rapidFireQAs.a: <34 weeks’ gestation if delivery would result in premature birth (i.e., do not use after 34 weeks); only able to delay birth up to a few days; terbutaline (beta-1/-2 agonist), ritodrine (beta-2 agonist), and nifedipine frequently used; notably effective in helping expectant mother to receive two boluses of corticosteroids in the 24-hour period prior to <34-week delivery; various contraindications, including infection, IUGR, and cervical dilation >4cm.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are Braxton-Hicks contractions
rapidFireQAs.a: irregular, spontaneous contractions sometimes felt in third trimester; they are normal and benign; in contrast, labor presents are regular and increasingly sustained contractions.

rapidFireQAs.q: When to give GBS prophylaxis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Hx of prior pregnancy with early-onset GBS disease in neonate (i.e., pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis); do not give if prior pregnancy demonstrated mere colonization of GBS. GBS bacteriuria at any point during current pregnancy (e.g., first trimester), even if treated successfully. Positive rectovaginal swab at 36 weeks. If maternal status is unknown, give if one or more of the following: Maternal fever >38C. ROM >18 hours. Preterm delivery (<37 weeks). Successful GBS prophylaxis is IV penicillin or ampicillin within 4 hours of delivery of fetus; oral amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) is the wrong answer. rapidFireQAs.q: Can you explain that annoying Bishop score stuff real quick?
rapidFireQAs.a: 5 criteria summing to 13 points; higher is better; >8 indicates likely successful vaginal delivery; <6 suggests cervical ripening may be required. USMLE will not make you calculate, don’t worry. But students sometimes ask about this. Cervical position: Posterior – 0 points; Middle – 1 point; Anterior – 2 points. Becomes more anterior as labor nears. Cervical consistency: Firm – 0 points; Medium – 1 point; Soft – 2 points. More rigid and resistant to stretch in primigravid women. Cervical effacement: 0-30% – 0 points; 30-50% – 1 point; 50-70% – 2 points; >70% – 3 points. How “thin” the cervix is; normally cervix is 3cm long; becomes “paper-thin” when fully effaced. Cervical dilation: Closed 0 points; 1-2cm – 1 point; 2-4cm – 2 points; >4cm – 3 points. Most important indicator of progression through first stage of labor. Fetal station: -3 – 0 points; -2 – 1 point; -1, 0 – 2 points; +1, +2 – 3 points. Fetal head position relative to ischial spines (usually 3-4cm intravaginal and non-palpable); - numbers mean the fetal head is above the ischial spines; + numbers mean head has descended below the ischial spines for impending delivery.

rapidFireQAs.q: Oh yeah can you quickly explain the fetal fibronectin test?
rapidFireQAs.a: fetal fibronectin (fFN) is the “glue” found between the chorion and decidua; if a woman is 22-35 weeks’ gestation and having symptoms of preterm labor, fFN test predicts whether preterm labor is likely; if negative, <5% chance of delivery within next two weeks; if positive, preterm labor likely.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + 33 weeks’ gestation + clear fluid leaking from vagina past two days + no contractions or bleeding; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: sterile speculum exam; likely preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM); wrong answers are fetal fibronectin test (only if premature labor / contractions).
